newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Shorter KL stocks settlement to have mixed impact.
newsitem.headline: Shorter KL stocks settlement to have mixed impact.

text.p: A contemplated shortening of the time period for stocks transaction settlements by Malaysian stock market regulators would have a mixed impact on the Kuala Lumpur bourse, dealers said on Tuesday.
In a circular sent to brokers dated August 28, the KLSE said it was considering the need to move to T+3 (transaction plus three days) from the current T+5.

A copy of the circular, obtained by Reuters, says the main objectives for the shorter settlement include minimising counterparty risk and market exposure and bringing Malaysia more in line with settlement time frames in other markets.
For example, the United States, Japan and France all practice T+3, while T+2 settlement is done in Hong Kong, Germany, Korea and Taiwan.

"Shorter settlement period reduces the time during which one party is exposed to the other and thus the time during which one party could fail and the time during which the market price could move in an unfavourable direction," the KLSE letter said.
The proposed shortening would also cut financing costs for broker firms, since they will have to bear the cost of buying the stocks for a shorter period.
The aspect of cutting risks is also appealing to the industry, said Richard Khoo, head of Malaysia's remisiers' association. Remisiers are freelance stockbrokers in Malaysia.

"Nobody talks about how much default there is in payments," he told Reuters on Tuesday. "This would be protecting my own remisiers," he said, adding that he believed there was enough liquidity in the market to support the proposed measure.
But a shorter settlement could at least initially hurt trading volumes as retail investors shy away from the smaller, speculative stocks, which have been a big part of the market's activity.
"Retailers will squeal annoyance and rage," said one institutional dealer with a local firm. "It will cut down on the opportunity for speculation."
"A lot of people trade on contra," said Ralph Dixon, of TA Securities's international division, referring to the contra period or the time during which a credit purchase of stock is done.
"It would reduce maybe 30 percent of the Second Board's volume, although I think it's being discounted already," he said.
And there have historically been worries that a shorter time frame would hurt earnings of the brokerage industry.
Jupiter Securities in its Tuesday research note pointed out that the Stock Exchange of Singapore shot down a similar proposal for precisely those reasons.
"Even if it was implemented in the future, the market would only weaken temporarily as contra players will just have to adjust to the new trading period," Jupiter said.
The firm added, "In Hongkong where the settlement period is even shorter, they still find plenty of contra players in their market."
